ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The superior vena cava (SVC) returns deoxygenated blood from the head, neck, upper limbs and thorax to the right atrium. Its position in the mediastinum makes it vulnerable to compression by tumours or thrombosis, producing the classic superior vena cava syndrome.

sections.p: The SVC is a short, thin‑walled vein that empties into the right atrium. It is the main conduit for venous return from the upper body.
b: Formed by the junction of the right and left brachiocephalic veins

sections.p: It lies in the superior mediastinum, posterior to the first right costal cartilage and anterior to the right main bronchus.
b: Runs vertically from the level of T1 to the right atrial border
Surrounded by pleura, thymus (in children) and lymph nodes

sections.p: Understanding neighbouring structures helps explain clinical signs when the SVC is compressed.
b: Posterior: right main bronchus, ascending aorta

sections.p: The SVC itself has no arterial supply; its wall receives tiny vasa vasorum from bronchial arteries.
Autonomic fibers from the vagus and sympathetic trunks accompany the mediastinal vessels, influencing venous tone.
Collects blood from the head, neck, upper limbs and thorax and delivers it to the right atrium, maintaining preload for the right ventricle.
Compression or thrombosis of the SVC produces superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS), a medical emergency.
b: Common causes: bronchogenic carcinoma, lymphoma, mediastinal metastases, indwelling catheters
Tropical considerations: TB mediastinal lymphadenitis, HIV‑related lymphoma, schistosomal fibrosis
Life‑threatening complications: airway obstruction, cerebral edema, hemodynamic collapse

t.b: Does it show mediastinal widening or a mass? A widened mediastinum suggests a compressive lesion.
What is the exact site and cause of obstruction? Identifies tumour, thrombus, or lymphadenopathy.
Is there a filling defect in the SVC? Demonstrates thrombosis when advanced imaging is not accessible.

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and bedside assessment.
b: Facial plethora, neck vein distension, and upper‑chest collateral veins = SVCS
Right atrial border on a PA chest film is the SVC above the atrium
Thrombosis risk ↑ with central lines, hypercoagulable states (e.g., sickle cell, HIV)

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden facial swelling with headache and dyspnea
Signs of airway compromise or altered mental status

faq.q: Why does SVCS cause facial swelling?
faq.a: Obstruction raises venous pressure upstream, forcing blood into superficial facial veins.

faq.q: Can a central venous catheter cause SVC obstruction?
faq.a: Yes, long‑term catheters can induce thrombosis or fibrosis leading to SVCS.

faq.q: Is SVCS always caused by cancer?
faq.a: No, infections (TB), thrombosis, and benign mediastinal masses can also produce it, especially in low‑resource settings.
